analysis.one_liner: Bars federal courts from ruling on state religion, privacy, and same-sex marriage laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee's courts subcommittee until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005, with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Supreme Court and all other federal courts from deciding any case involving state laws on religion, privacy (including abortion, sexual practices, and reproduction), or same-sex marriage. It would also void federal court precedents on those topics as binding authority in state courts, and would make it an impeachable offense for a judge to rule on them anyway. The practical effect: state legislatures could pass laws on school prayer, abortion, and marriage that federal courts could no longer strike down.
analysis.who_benefits: State legislatures and governors, who would regain the power to regulate religion, abortion, sexual orientation, and marriage without any federal constitutional check. Religious-conservative state policymakers in particular could enact school prayer, establishment, abortion, and marriage laws that current federal precedent (like Roe v. Wade and Lawrence v. Texas) blocks. No federal court order could compel a state to spend money or change its laws on these subjects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State legislatures and conservative state policymakers

how_it_helps.text: Strips federal courts of the power to decide any claim about state laws on the free exercise or establishment of religion, privacy and reproduction, or the right to marry without regard to sex or sexual orientation.
Bars federal courts from issuing any order that spends money, imposes taxes, or interferes with the legislative or administrative functions of state governments.
Makes federal decisions on those removed topics no longer binding precedent on state courts, undoing the state-level effect of rulings the bill's findings attack, such as abortion decisions.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people in states that restrict these rights. Anyone whose privacy, reproductive freedom, religious liberty, or equal protection claim against a state government would currently go to federal court would lose that forum, leaving only state courts whose rulings on these subjects could not be reviewed federally.
analysis.who_pays_short: People suing states over privacy and religion rights

drawbacks.text: It removes the federal courts as a backstop for individuals challenging state laws on religion, privacy, abortion, and same-sex marriage, so a state law on those subjects could stand no matter what the federal Constitution says about it.
It declares that any judge who rules on a barred topic has committed an impeachable offense and is subject to removal, which critics would see as a direct threat to judicial independence.
It voids federal precedent on the covered issues for state courts, which would create a patchwork where the same individual right depends on which state a person lives in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters frame this as restoring democratic control: the bill's own findings argue that elected state governments, not unelected federal judges, should decide these questions under the Tenth Amendment. The cost falls on individuals: anyone who loses a privacy, abortion, religious-liberty, or marriage dispute with their state government would have no federal court to appeal to, and the threat of impeachment for judges who rule anyway goes well beyond the usual checks on courts. The bill also does nothing procedural to fix how such laws are made; it simply removes one forum of review.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its courts subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on March 4, 2004, with Rep. Roscoe Bartlett as its only cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on June 28, 2004, referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on federal courts to check state laws on religion, abortion, and marriage are better off, since federal jurisdiction over those claims stayed intact. The federal judiciary also kept its authority, and state governments did not gain the unchecked power the bill would have handed them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal court rights protections

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the We the People Act to strip federal court jurisdiction over state religion, privacy, and marriage laws.

for.name: Rep. Roscoe Bartlett
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Standing committee of the U.S. House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never reported the bill out; it was sent to the courts subcommittee on June 28, 2004, and never acted on further.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill hands state governments unchecked power over religion, abortion, sexual orientation, and marriage by removing federal court review, exactly the outcome the bill's findings call for. People whose individual rights clash with state policy on those subjects would have nowhere to challenge the laws.

Federal courts would lose jurisdiction over a broad category of constitutional claims, and a judge who ruled anyway would face impeachment and removal. This is an institutional loss of power rather than an economic one.
